Different source types have different APA formats: a book entry includes the publisher, while a journal article entry includes the journal name, volume, issue, page range, and DOI where available.
Plagiarism is the presentation of someone else's work or ideas as your own, whether by copying, paraphrasing without attribution, or submitting work done by another person.
Self-plagiarism—submitting your own previously assessed work as though it were new—is also a form of academic dishonesty.

Strategies for avoiding plagiarism include taking careful notes that distinguish your own ideas from source material, citing every borrowed idea even when paraphrased, and using plagiarism-detection tools before submission.

definitions.definition: A formal acknowledgement, embedded within your text or placed at the end of your document, that identifies the source of an idea, fact, or quotation you have used. In APA style, an in-text citation takes the form (Surname, Year).

A brief reference inserted in the body of your writing at the point where you use borrowed material. In APA style it gives the author's surname and publication year in parentheses—and a page number if you are quoting directly—so the reader can match it to the full entry in the reference list.

A complete, alphabetically ordered list of all sources cited in a document, placed at the end of the work. Each entry provides enough information (author, year, title, publisher or journal details) for the reader to locate the original source. In APA style, entries use a hanging indent.

A referencing and formatting system published by the American Psychological Association. It uses an author–date citation method and prescribes exact formats for in-text citations and reference list entries depending on the source type (book, journal article, website, etc.).

The word-for-word reproduction of a source's exact language, enclosed in double quotation marks. In APA style, a direct quotation requires the author's surname, year, and page number: (Okafor, 2019, p. 78). Quotations of 40 words or more are formatted as indented block quotations without quotation marks.

A restatement of a source's idea in your own words and sentence structure, roughly similar in length to the original. A paraphrase demonstrates your understanding of the material and still requires an in-text citation, though no page number is mandatory in APA style.

The act of presenting another person's words, ideas, data, or creative work as your own without proper acknowledgement, whether intentional or accidental. It includes copying text, paraphrasing without citation, submitting purchased or ghostwritten work, and re-using your own previously submitted work without permission (self-plagiarism).

The commitment to honesty, fairness, and responsibility in all academic work. It requires that students produce their own original work, acknowledge all sources used, and neither give nor receive unauthorised assistance. Violations can result in penalties ranging from a zero grade to expulsion.

workedExamples.title: Writing APA in-text citations for a quotation and a paraphrase
workedExamples.problem: You are writing an essay and wish to use material from the following source: a book titled 'Foundations of Academic Writing' by Ngozi Uche, published in 2020 by Lagos University Press. On page 34, Uche writes: 'Academic writing demands that every borrowed idea, however small, be traced to its origin.' You want to (a) quote this sentence directly, and (b) paraphrase the same idea. Write the correct APA in-text citation for each case.
steps: Identify the citation elements needed. For any APA in-text citation you need at minimum: author's surname and year of publication. For a direct quotation you also need the page number.

Write the direct quotation. Copy the exact words and enclose them in double quotation marks. Place the citation—surname, year, page number—in parentheses immediately after the closing quotation mark and before the full stop: 'Academic writing demands that every borrowed idea, however small, be traced to its origin' (Uche, 2020, p. 34).

Write the paraphrase. Recast the idea completely in your own words without looking at the original sentence. For example: 'In academic writing, even the smallest idea taken from another source must be properly attributed.' Now add the in-text citation after the sentence, but without a page number, since APA style does not require one for paraphrases: (Uche, 2020).

Check both citations. Both use Surname, Year format. The quotation adds p. 34; the paraphrase does not. Neither citation begins with 'p.' for the year, and there is no comma between surname and year in the in-text form—only between year and page number.
workedExamples.answer: (a) Direct quotation: 'Academic writing demands that every borrowed idea, however small, be traced to its origin' (Uche, 2020, p. 34). (b) Paraphrase: In academic writing, even the smallest idea taken from another source must be properly attributed (Uche, 2020).

workedExamples.title: Constructing APA reference list entries for a book and a journal article
workedExamples.problem: Compile correctly formatted APA 7th-edition reference list entries for the following two sources. Source 1 — Book: Author: Emeka Eze; Year: 2018; Title: Research Methods in the Social Sciences; Publisher: Ibadan Academic Press. Source 2 — Journal article: Authors: Fatima Bello and Samuel Adio; Year: 2022; Article title: 'Critical thinking skills in Nigerian higher education'; Journal: Journal of African Education; Volume: 15; Issue: 3; Pages: 102–119; DOI: 10.1000/jae.2022.153.
steps: Recall the APA format for a book: Author, A. A. (Year). Title of work in italics: Subtitle if any. Publisher. Note: only the first word of the title and any proper nouns are capitalised (sentence case).

Apply this to Source 1: Eze, E. (2018). Research methods in the social sciences. Ibadan Academic Press. Explanation: 'Research methods in the social sciences' is in italics and sentence case; the author's initials follow the surname; the year is in parentheses; the entry ends with the publisher's name only (no 'Ltd' or location required in APA 7).
Recall the APA format for a journal article: Author, A. A., & Author, B. B. (Year). Title of article in sentence case. Title of Journal in Italics, Volume(Issue), page–page. https://doi.org/xxxxx

Apply this to Source 2: Bello, F., & Adio, S. (2022). Critical thinking skills in Nigerian higher education. Journal of African Education, 15(3), 102–119. https://doi.org/10.1000/jae.2022.153 Note: the journal name and volume number are italicised; the issue number in parentheses is not italicised; the article title is in sentence case (only the first word capitalised); the ampersand (&) is used between authors.

Arrange both entries in alphabetical order by the first author's surname. Bello comes before Eze, so Source 2 appears first. Apply a hanging indent (the first line is flush left; subsequent lines are indented by 0.5 inches/1.27 cm).
workedExamples.answer:
Reference list (alphabetical order, hanging indent applied):

Bello, F., & Adio, S. (2022). Critical thinking skills in Nigerian higher education. Journal of African Education, 15(3), 102–119. https://doi.org/10.1000/jae.2022.153

Eze, E. (2018). Research methods in the social sciences. Ibadan Academic Press.

workedExamples.title: Identifying and correcting plagiarism in a student's paragraph
workedExamples.problem: A student found the following sentence in a source (Akinola, 2019, p. 12): 'Corruption undermines institutional trust, weakens governance structures, and ultimately retards national development.' The student wrote this in their essay: 'Corruption undermines institutional trust, weakens governance structures, and ultimately slows down national development.' No citation was provided. Explain why this is plagiarism and rewrite the passage in two acceptable ways: (a) as a properly cited direct quotation, and (b) as a properly cited paraphrase.
steps: Diagnose the problem. The student changed only one phrase ('retards national development' → 'slows down national development') and kept the rest of the sentence identical. This is a classic example of patchwriting—minimal word substitution without genuine restatement—and it lacks any citation. It is plagiarism because the structure, sequence of ideas, and most of the wording are still Akinola's, and the source is not acknowledged.

Write an acceptable direct quotation (Option a). Copy the original words exactly, enclose them in quotation marks, and add the full APA in-text citation including the page number: According to Akinola (2019), 'Corruption undermines institutional trust, weakens governance structures, and ultimately retards national development' (p. 12).

Write an acceptable paraphrase (Option b). Step away from the original, think about the core idea—corruption damages trust in institutions, makes governing harder, and holds back a country's progress—and write that idea in a completely different structure: When corruption takes hold, citizens lose faith in public institutions, the ability of governments to function is compromised, and the nation's prospects for development are significantly diminished (Akinola, 2019). Notice that the sentence structure, order of ideas, and vocabulary are genuinely different.

Confirm that both versions are free of plagiarism. Option (a) is legitimate because the quotation marks signal that the words are not the student's own, and the citation credits the source. Option (b) is legitimate because the wording is genuinely original and the citation still credits the idea to Akinola.
workedExamples.answer: Plagiarism diagnosis: The student's version is patchwriting—only one word was changed, the sentence structure is identical to the original, and there is no citation. Acceptable rewrite (a) — Direct quotation: According to Akinola (2019), 'Corruption undermines institutional trust, weakens governance structures, and ultimately retards national development' (p. 12). Acceptable rewrite (b) — Paraphrase: When corruption takes hold, citizens lose faith in public institutions, the ability of governments to function is compromised, and the nation's prospects for development are significantly diminished (Akinola, 2019).

quiz.question: A student quotes directly from page 56 of a 2017 book by an author with the surname Dada. Which in-text citation is correctly formatted in APA style?
quiz.explanation: APA in-text citations for direct quotations use the format (Surname, Year, p. Page), with commas between each element and the lowercase abbreviation 'p.' for page—not 'pg.' and not reordered.

quiz.question: When constructing an APA reference list entry for a journal article, which element is written in italics?
options: The article title
The authors' surnames
The journal name and volume number
The issue number and page range
quiz.explanation: In APA style, the journal name and the volume number are italicised; the article title is in plain sentence case, and the issue number (in parentheses) and page range are not italicised.

quiz.question: A student rewrites a paragraph from a source, changes most of the words but keeps exactly the same sentence structure, and adds a citation. Which statement best describes this practice?
options: It is fully acceptable because a citation has been provided.
It is a direct quotation and needs quotation marks.
It is patchwriting and may still constitute plagiarism because the sentence structure is not genuinely original.
It is self-plagiarism because the student reused their own earlier work.
quiz.explanation: Patchwriting—substituting words while retaining the original sentence structure—does not constitute a genuine paraphrase; even with a citation, it can be judged as plagiarism because the expression has not been made truly original.

quiz.question: Which of the following is an example of self-plagiarism?
options: Copying a paragraph from a classmate's essay
Quoting a source without quotation marks
Submitting an essay you wrote for a different course as a new assignment without your lecturer's permission
Forgetting to include a reference list entry for a source you cited in the text
quiz.explanation: Self-plagiarism occurs when a student presents their own previously submitted work as new original work; reusing an essay from another course without disclosure and permission is the clearest example of this violation.
